name: Streaming OLAP / 'real-time enough'
parent_research_topic: Beava's current market position — competitor archetypes and market segments beava is positioned in or against, evaluated against the use-case map in ../beava-use-cases/

competitive_landscape.incumbents: Real-time / streaming OLAP databases: ClickHouse (Apache-2.0, ClickHouse Inc. with Cloud open-core), Apache Pinot (Apache-2.0, ASF, commercialized by StarTree — $75M total funding, $47M Series B in 2022), Apache Druid (Apache-2.0, ASF, commercialized by Imply), StarRocks (Apache-2.0, Linux Foundation, commercialized by CelerData — ~$60M+ raised), Apache Doris, Tinybird (proprietary platform on top of ClickHouse — $30M Series B June 2024 at $240M valuation), Hydrolix ($80M Series C April 2025, streaming data lake; >650 customers, 8x revenue growth in 2024), Imply Polaris (managed Druid), StarTree Cloud (managed Pinot), CelerData (managed StarRocks). All target sub-second ad-hoc analytical SQL on freshly ingested event streams. Cross-cutting horizontal: Snowflake Dynamic Tables, BigQuery streaming + materialized views, Databricks Real-Time Mode have crept into the same 'real-time enough' (1–60s lag) territory. The category is structurally an ad-hoc-SQL-on-streams play, not a per-entity feature server.
competitive_landscape.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: For use case 5 (behavioral analytics live): ClickHouse is the dominant choice (PostHog runs on it, Tinybird's hero use case — Vercel uses Tinybird for real-time web analytics, FanDuel for live sportsbook user-facing analytics, Canva for product analytics; Mixpanel/Amplitude-class vendors typically run ClickHouse internally). Apache Druid is the classic Pivot-style live-product-dashboard backend (Confluent, Netflix). StarTree (Pinot) targets the LinkedIn-style 'who-viewed-my-profile' user-facing analytics shape. For use case 14 (observability — per-tenant/per-route rolling rates): ClickStack (ClickHouse-backed observability, HyperDX/SigNoz/Uptrace/OpenObserve are the OSS stacks; ClickHouse's own December 2025 ClickStack release ships per-tenant streaming materialized views), Hydrolix (named Data Observability Innovation of the Year 2025; supported the 2025 Super Bowl with ~200TB ingest in hours, 10s time-to-glass for FOX Sports), StarTree's observability play (announced Sep 2024), Imply Lumi (released Sep 2025 as 'decoupled data layer for observability'). Tinybird and StarRocks 4.0 (Sep 2025, 60% faster query, Iceberg integration) are aggressively pushing into the same 'streaming observability' niche. Funding/M&A summary (2024–2026): Tinybird $30M Series B June 2024; Hydrolix $80M Series C April 2025; StarTree Series B $47M 2022 (no later round confirmed); StarRocks/CelerData no public 2025 raise confirmed [uncertain]; Imply Lumi launched Sep 2025; ClickHouse Cloud continues aggressive AWS/Azure/GCP marketplace bundling and HIPAA-compliant rollout.
competitive_landscape.oss_license_posture: Mixed. The open-source engines (ClickHouse core, Apache Pinot, Apache Druid, StarRocks, Apache Doris) are all Apache-2.0 — same license as beava. ClickHouse Inc. is showing open-core drift: SharedMergeTree (cloud-native storage-compute separation) and lightweight UPDATE are ClickHouse Cloud-only, raising 'is ClickHouse moving away from open source?' concerns (Altinity blog, 2024–2025); ClickHouse remains formally Apache-2.0 but key 2025 features ship cloud-only. Pinot and Druid are pure ASF projects (vendor-neutral). StarRocks is Linux Foundation (vendor-neutral). Tinybird is proprietary (March 14 2025 self-managed license is source-available, not OSI-approved). Hydrolix is proprietary. Net: the OSS engines are license-clean and not a competitive license wedge for beava; the managed platforms (Tinybird, Hydrolix, Imply Polaris, StarTree Cloud, ClickHouse Cloud) are where lock-in risk lives.
competitive_landscape.hyperscaler_bundling_threat: High. This is the single most predictive structural factor in this segment. Snowflake Dynamic Tables (1-minute minimum target lag, GA 2024), BigQuery streaming + materialized views, Databricks Real-Time Mode (announced Data+AI Summit 2025), and AWS Redshift Streaming Ingestion now cover the 'real-time enough' (1–60s freshness) regime for buyers who already pay a hyperscaler. ClickHouse Cloud is itself a hyperscaler-marketplace play (cross-org marketplace billing consolidation across AWS/Azure/GCP shipped 2025–2026). Confluent + Flink + Snowflake or Confluent + Tinybird is now a one-line marketplace add-on for buyers on either side. A buyer evaluating 'do I need real-time analytics?' will reach for a marketplace bundle 80%+ of the time. The exception is the user-facing-analytics niche where sub-second latency and 50–1000 QPS concurrency push them off Snowflake/BigQuery into ClickHouse/Pinot/Tinybird — but that is still cloud-native, not single-binary OSS territory.
competitive_landscape.integration_surface: Kafka-first by default. Pinot ingests from Kafka, Pulsar, Kinesis natively. Druid has native Kafka/Kinesis with query-on-arrival semantics at millions of events/sec. ClickHouse has Kafka table engine + Materialized Views as the canonical streaming-ingest pattern; Tinybird ships Kafka/Confluent connectors as a marquee feature. StarRocks supports Kafka + batch + Iceberg. Hydrolix ingests from CDN HTTP logs, Cloudflare, Mux Data, Kafka. The buyer expectation in this segment is 'point a Kafka topic at it and write SQL' — beava's HTTP-push / TCP+msgpack model is a friction here for the streaming-OLAP buyer, who already has a Kafka bus and expects to wire it directly. Beava fits better when the buyer wants a sidecar next to the event collector rather than a topic consumer. Conversely, OTel-collector → HTTP exporter and Envoy access-log tail (the use-case-14 producer paths) map cleanly onto beava's HTTP/TCP push model — friction with Kafka, fit with the gateway/agent ingest path.
competitive_landscape.scoring_engine_coupling: Mostly external. Streaming OLAP is read-by-dashboards and read-by-alerters, not by inline ML scorers. Buyers run Grafana / Metabase / Superset / in-house React dashboards on top, and Alertmanager / PagerDuty Event Intelligence / Grafana Alerting on the side. Inline rules engines are rare; inline ML scorers are essentially absent — the latency profile (10ms–1s queries) is wrong for inline gating. This is exactly where beava is structurally different: beava sits in the data path with sub-ms gets feeding XGBoost / ONNX / contextual bandits at decision time, OLAP sits in the analyst / alerting path.

beava_position_lens.beava_credible_wedge: Beava and streaming OLAP are not the same product — they serve different verbs (per-entity get vs ad-hoc aggregate SQL) at different latency budgets (sub-ms point lookup at 10k–100k+ QPS vs 10ms–1s ad-hoc aggregate at 50–500 QPS concurrency). Public ClickHouse benchmarks state ~4K lookups/sec on MergeTree tables and ~10K via Dictionary tables — and the ClickHouse docs themselves say 'not suitable for a high load of simple point queries' because each key forces a granule scan and column decompression. Pinot/Druid have the same shape. That gap is beava's credible wedge for the in-path feature-serving role: a single beava binary serves the rolling per-(user_id, route, tenant_id) feature vector to a real-time decision (personalization gate, rate-limit, anomaly trigger) in <1ms, while the OLAP backend remains the analyst surface alongside. Apache-2.0 with no open-core (vs ClickHouse Cloud's SharedMergeTree split) is a secondary wedge for vendors who don't want to lock the hot tier into a cloud-only feature. Single binary with WAL + snapshot (no Kafka, no Flink, no Kubernetes-cluster-of-coordinators-and-historicals as Druid requires) is the third wedge for buyers who want a sidecar, not an architecture. The 50+ aggregation primitives (count, n_unique, velocity, recency, t-digest, EWMA, HLL) cover the rolling-window features both use cases 5 and 14 live on, computed at ingest time per entity rather than scanned at query time.
beava_position_lens.beava_disqualifiers: Beava cannot replace a streaming OLAP system in its actual job: ad-hoc SQL exploration, funnels, cohorts, paths, joins across tenant × route × time × user, retroactive event redefinition (Heap-style), high-concurrency dashboards with 50–500 dimensions selectable. v0 has no SQL surface, no joins, no cross-entity aggregation at query time, no ad-hoc filtering — features are precomputed declaratively or they don't exist. Beava cannot serve a 28-day SLO compliance roll-up (in-memory only, no long-term tier). Beava cannot serve the analyst surface that Mixpanel/Amplitude/PostHog/Grafana sit on top of. Beava has no Kafka native ingest, no Iceberg/Parquet sink, no Grafana data-source plugin, no Prometheus remote-write receiver, no OTel-collector exporter — every one of these is table-stakes for an OLAP buyer. No TLS / auth in v0. No in-process sharding above ~684k EPS / ~50GB hot state per node. No multi-tenancy primitives (namespaces, per-tenant quotas) that Mimir, Pinot, and ClickHouse Cloud all ship. The buyer mismatch is the dominant story: an OLAP buyer is an analyst / SRE / dashboard team asking 'let me write SQL on fresh events'; a beava buyer is a risk / personalization / platform team asking 'serve me this feature on the next request in <1ms'.
beava_position_lens.time_to_credible_offering: 12mo+ — and only if the goal is 'compete in this segment.' For 'coexist as the hot per-entity tier in front of an OLAP backend' the time is 3-6mo (TLS/auth + OTel exporter + Kafka consumer + Parquet/Iceberg sink + documented OLAP-coexistence reference architecture). Replacing a streaming OLAP system is not realistically on the table for v0 or v1; the SQL / ad-hoc / joins surface alone is 12+ months of work and would invalidate the events-only / no-joins / processing-time-only locked invariants in SOURCE-OF-TRUTH.md.

evidence_and_verdict.validation_signals_today: No public beava users in this segment identified [uncertain]. The streaming OLAP segment is a published-customer-rich incumbent space: ClickHouse Inc. publishes HighLevel, Mux, Poizon enterprise case studies; PostHog ships on ClickHouse with public per-tenant event-volume numbers; Tinybird publishes Vercel, Canva, FanDuel customer stories with explicit user-facing analytics framing; Hydrolix publishes TF1 multi-CDN observability, FOX Sports Super Bowl 2025 200TB-in-hours; StarTree publishes 1B queries/week. Beava's repo contains demos for ecommerce / fraud / personalization shape (python/beava/demos/ecommerce) but no purpose-built behavioral-analytics-rolling-counters or per-tenant-rolling-RED-metrics demo. The closest validation signal is structural — beava's count/n_unique/velocity/recency/HLL primitives map 1:1 onto the rolling-counter workload that ClickHouse + Tinybird customers build by hand with materialized views. No beava-specific Discord / GitHub thread on streaming OLAP coexistence located [uncertain].
evidence_and_verdict.verdict: Avoid as a head-to-head replacement; Watch as coexistence partner. Streaming OLAP is the wrong frame for beava — different verb (per-entity get vs ad-hoc aggregate SQL), different buyer (platform/risk/personalization vs analyst/SRE), different latency budget (sub-ms point read vs 10ms–1s aggregate scan). Do not chase 'replace ClickHouse / Pinot / Druid'. Do invest in a credible coexistence story (OTel exporter + Kafka consumer + Parquet sink + 'beava in front of ClickHouse' reference architecture) so a buyer can run beava as the hot per-entity tier while keeping their existing OLAP backend as the analyst surface.
